idiom_name: Play controller action per route (Action { request => ... })
implementation_notes: Play expresses the page controller as an Action: a controller class generates one Action value per route (def index = Action { request => Ok(views.html.orders(...)) }) and the routes file maps each URL to that method, so the mapping and the handler are separate artifacts; the classic controller base class is supplied by AbstractController and shared behaviour by action composition (ActionBuilder) or filters. http4s is the functional sibling: HttpRoutes.of[IO] pattern-matches Request values and returns F[Response] with no controller objects at all. Prefer Play for conventional page-oriented applications and http4s when the whole stack is cats-effect based.
pitfalls: Actions execute per request on shared controller instances: values captured by the class are application-global, not per page view.
The routes file is the only place URLs exist: an action without a route compiles but never serves, and editing a route silently changes the public URL contract.
Blocking JDBC or filesystem calls inside an Action run on Play's default execution context and starve it - wrap them in a dedicated dispatcher or return async results.

variants.name: http4s HttpRoutes (pattern match on Request)
variants.implementation_notes: The pure-functional realization: there are no controller objects - an HttpRoutes[IO] is a partial function from Request to F[Response], so each page is one case in the pattern match and the effect type carries the side effects. Middleware is a Kleisli transformation or route composition and the Router mounts the result; prefer it when the application is effect-based end to end, because mixing it with OO controllers throws away the abstraction's value.
variants.code_sketch:
val ordersRoutes = HttpRoutes.of[IO] {
  case GET -> Root / "orders" =>
    orderService.list().flatMap(page => Ok(renderOrders(page)))   // domain + view
  case req @ POST -> Root / "orders" =>
    req.as[OrderForm].flatMap(placeOrder) *> SeeOther("/orders")
}
val app = Router("/" -> ordersRoutes).orNotFound
pitfalls: Errors are values in F: an unhandled failure becomes a 500 through the middleware, so each route must map expected failures to explicit responses.
Routes form a partial function, so an unmatched request falls through to the router's fallback; a catch-all case placed early hides every later page.
Interpretation is deferred until the server runs the IO, so request-scoped side effects written in the match itself (rather than in F) run at the wrong time.
